/ The problem

Heating and cooling make up most of a school’s energy use.

42%of energy in U.S. education buildings goes to space heating
11%goes to cooling
2% to 5%of a building’s energy for every 1°C the thermostat setpoint moves, in two published studies of office buildings

Sources: U.S. EIA, Commercial Buildings Energy Consumption Survey; Saurav et al., Luleå field trial; HVAC operational strategies study. Details in the calculator below.

/ Our story

“In some classrooms I need to wear a sweatshirt even in the middle of winter, while in the next hallway it’s so hot you can’t focus.”

A Millburn High School student

Desert to tundra, all in one building. We built ECHO to find out where the energy is going.

/ How it works

Measure it, see it, fix it.

Step 1

Plug in a sensor

InstaHub’s Plug n’ Play sensors collect data every 10 minutes on motion, CO₂, temperature, humidity, light and air pressure.

Step 2

Spot the waste

An online dashboard tracks vacancy, lighting waste and heating waste in each room, so we can find patterns and recommend ways to cut unnecessary energy use.

Step 3

Act on it

Students use the data to brainstorm ways to be more energy efficient. ECHO is also being built into Millburn High School’s Applied Integrated CS class.

/ See it in action

Peel, plug in, done.

The sensor goes on the wall and plugs into an outlet. From there it picks up things like light usage and room activity and sends them to the dashboard.

/ Backed by research

Buildings waste energy in ways nobody can see.

25%

In one elementary school study, about 416 of the 1,694 kWh of weekly lighting energy went to rooms with nobody in them.

Floyd et al., 1996
53%

Space heating takes 42% and cooling 11% of the energy used in U.S. education buildings.

U.S. EIA, Commercial Buildings Energy Consumption Survey
5.2%

A field trial in Luleå, Sweden found about 5.2% of a building’s energy use for every 1°C of heating setpoint change.

Luleå pilot trial
27%

A Berkeley study found about 27% of HVAC energy saved with a 2.8°C wider setpoint range.

UC Berkeley, Center for the Built Environment
1.9%

A hot-climate office simulation found about 1.9% of electricity saved per 1°C of setpoint change.

HVAC operational strategies study

/ Try it

What does an off-target thermostat cost?

Enter your building and how far rooms drift from comfortable to get a yearly estimate.

Defaults are New Jersey commercial averages. Your utility bill has your real rates.
Wasted energy cost per year… CO₂ released per year…
How this is calculated, and where the numbers come from
  1. Total energy: square feet × 62.7 kBtu per square foot, the average for U.S. education buildings (EIA CBECS).
  2. Waste per degree: 5.2% of total building energy per 1°C of setpoint offset (about 2.9% per °F). That is the result of a field trial in Luleå, Sweden (5.23%). A rough check against a Berkeley study agrees: it found 27% of HVAC energy saved for a 2.8°C setpoint change, and heating and cooling are about 53% of a school’s energy, which works out to about 5.1% per °C. A hot-climate simulation found as little as 1.9%, so milder climates may see less.
  3. Fuel split: 57% electricity, 43% natural gas, from EIA’s national education totals (437 and 328 trillion Btu).
  4. Cost: kWh × your electricity price, plus therms × your gas price. Defaults: about 17¢ per kWh (EIA commercial average for NJ, 12 months to July 2026) and $11.58 per thousand cubic feet, or about $1.13 per therm (EIA, NJ commercial gas, 2024).
  5. CO₂: natural gas at 53.06 kg per mmBtu (EPA Emission Factors Hub). Electricity at 1,278.7 lb per MWh, the non-baseload rate for the RFC East grid region that covers New Jersey, which EPA recommends for estimating reductions (EPA eGRID2022).

Limits: the studies above looked at office buildings, not schools, and results vary a lot by climate and HVAC system. Treat this as an estimate for comparing options, not a bill prediction.
